pendulum.title: Simple Pendulum
pendulum.description: Observe the periodic motion of a simple pendulum.
pendulum.physics: The motion is governed by the restoring force of gravity, resulting in a simple harmonic motion for small angles.

double-pendulum.title: Double Pendulum
double-pendulum.description: Explore the chaotic motion of a double pendulum system.
double-pendulum.physics: A double pendulum is a pendulum with another pendulum attached to its end, and is a simple physical system which exhibits rich dynamic behavior with a strong sensitivity to initial conditions.

projectile-motion.title: Projectile Motion
projectile-motion.description: Simulate the trajectory of an object in a gravitational field.
projectile-motion.physics: Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown into the air, subject to the acceleration of gravity and optional air resistance.

n-body-orbit.title: N-Body Orbit
n-body-orbit.description: Visualize the gravitational interaction between multiple celestial bodies.
n-body-orbit.physics: The N-body problem involves predicting the individual motions of a group of celestial objects interacting with each other gravitationally.

electric-field.title: Electric Field Visualizer
electric-field.description: Map the electric field lines generated by multiple point charges.
electric-field.physics: Electric field lines provide a way to visualize the influence of electric charges in the space surrounding them.

wave-superposition.title: Wave Superposition
wave-superposition.description: Observe the interference patterns created by overlapping waves.
wave-superposition.physics: Wave superposition occurs when two or more waves overlap, resulting in a net displacement that is the sum of the individual displacements.

brownian-motion.title: Brownian Motion
brownian-motion.description: Simulate the random motion of particles in a fluid.
brownian-motion.physics: Brownian motion describes the random movement of particles suspended in a medium, caused by collisions with atoms or molecules.

gauss-law.title: Gauss's Law Visualizer
gauss-law.description: Place charges inside or outside a closed surface to observe the net electric flux.
gauss-law.physics: Gauss's Law states that the net electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the total enclosed electric charge. Flux depends only on the interior charges.

spacetime-relativity.title: Minkowski Spacetime Diagram
spacetime-relativity.description: Explore how relative motion warps space and time coordinates, visualizing length contraction and time dilation in real-time.
spacetime-relativity.physics: A Minkowski spacetime diagram maps events in space and time relative to different observers. According to Special Relativity, as an observer's velocity approaches the speed of light, their coordinate axes warp (rotate symmetrically inward toward the light cone). This simulation demonstrates coordinate grids, length contraction, and time dilation under Lorentz transformations.

wavefunction-tunneling.title: Quantum Tunneling & Schrödinger Well
wavefunction-tunneling.description: Visualize a probability wave packet colliding with a potential barrier, demonstrating reflection, transmission, and quantum tunneling.
wavefunction-tunneling.physics: Quantum tunneling is a quantum mechanical phenomenon where a particle transition occurs through a potential barrier that it classically could not surmount. The wave function decays exponentially inside the barrier and emerges on the other side with a reduced amplitude, representing a non-zero probability of finding the particle beyond the barrier.

vortex-street.title: Kármán Vortex Street
vortex-street.description: Simulate fluid flowing past a cylindrical obstacle, demonstrating the chaotic generation of alternating vortex shedding.
vortex-street.physics: A Kármán vortex street is a repeating pattern of swirling vortices, caused by the unsteady separation of flow of a fluid around blunted bodies. This phenomenon is governed by the Reynolds number, where laminar flow transitions into alternating vortex shedding structures under non-linear fluid dynamics.

gravitational-lensing.title: Schwarzschild Gravitational Lensing
gravitational-lensing.description: Visualize gravitational light bending and Einstein rings around a Schwarzschild black hole using relativistic ray-tracing.
gravitational-lensing.physics: In general relativity, light paths are bent by gravity. Photons travel along null geodesics in the Schwarzschild metric of a static, spherical mass. As light from background stars passes near a black hole, it is deflected. For alignment along the line of sight, this produces a ring of light (Einstein Ring) or multiple distorted images.

path-integral.title: Feynman Path Integral
path-integral.description: Visualize quantum sum-over-histories by accumulating phase vectors along hundreds of random paths, illustrating the classical limit.
path-integral.physics: In the path integral formulation of quantum mechanics, a particle travels from source to destination along all possible paths simultaneously. Each path is assigned a probability amplitude phase factor e^(iS/ħ), where S is the action. Summing these phase factors over all paths yields the transition probability. As Planck's constant ħ approaches zero, non-classical paths interfere destructively, leaving only the classical trajectory of least action.

maxwells-demon.title: Maxwell's Demon
maxwells-demon.description: Observe the thermodynamic paradox of Maxwell's Demon sorting gas molecules between two chambers, violating the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and resolve it using information entropy.
maxwells-demon.physics: In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell proposed a thought experiment where a microscopic "demon" guards a door between two gas chambers. By opening the door only for fast molecules to enter one side and slow molecules the other, the demon reduces thermal entropy without doing work, seemingly violating the Second Law. This paradox is resolved by noting that the demon must store information about the molecules, and erasing this memory generates entropy (Landauer's Principle).

bells-inequality.title: Bell's Inequality Locality Test
bells-inequality.description: Recreate the EPR thought experiment and measure polarization correlations between entangled photon pairs to violate local realism, testing Bell's and CHSH inequalities.
bells-inequality.physics: In 1935, Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen (EPR) proposed that quantum mechanics was incomplete, arguing for "local hidden variables." In 1964, John Stewart Bell proved that local realist theories place a strict upper bound on the correlation of distant measurements. Entangled quantum particles violate this bound. By measuring spin correlations of entangled photon pairs along detector angles a and b, this simulation tests local realism against quantum mechanics, violating the CHSH inequality |S| <= 2 and reaching the Tsirelson bound of 2√2.

geodesic-tracer.title: Curved Spacetime Geodesic Tracer
geodesic-tracer.description: Trace particle and photon trajectories around static or rotating black holes, exploring event horizons, photon spheres, and frame-dragging in Schwarzschild and Kerr geometries.
geodesic-tracer.physics: This simulation solves the general relativistic geodesic equations of motion in the equatorial plane of a black hole. In Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, the paths of particles and light are integrated using a Runge-Kutta 4th-order (RK4) method. For a static black hole (Schwarzschild metric, spin a=0), orbits precess (Einstein precession) and light is bent. For a rotating black hole (Kerr metric, spin a > 0), the spacetime itself is dragged in the direction of the rotation (frame-dragging or Lense-Thirring effect), warping orbits and forming an ergosphere.

relativistic-black-hole.title: Relativistic Kerr Black Hole Raytracer
relativistic-black-hole.description: Interactive GPU-accelerated general relativistic null geodesic raytracer around Schwarzschild and rotating Kerr black holes, modeling event horizons, photon spheres, ergospheres, and accretion disk Doppler beaming.
relativistic-black-hole.physics: General relativity describes gravity as the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime induced by mass and energy. Around a stationary or spinning black hole, spacetime geometry is determined by the vacuum Einstein field equations $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$, yielding the static Schwarzschild metric (spin $a = 0$) or the axisymmetric Kerr metric ($a > 0$). Light rays follow null geodesics ($ds^2 = 0$) governed by the geodesic equation. Photons approaching within the critical impact parameter are captured into the event horizon $r_+ = M + \sqrt{M^2 - a^2}$, casting the central black hole shadow bordered by the bright photon ring ($r = 3M$ in Schwarzschild). In Kerr geometry, the rotation of the singularity drags spacetime itself (the Lense-Thirring effect), creating an ergosphere $r_{\text{ergo}} = M + \sqrt{M^2 - a^2 \cos^2\theta}$ where no object can remain stationary relative to infinity. Infalling gas forms a Keplerian accretion disk whose emission is strongly distorted by gravitational redshift and relativistic Doppler beaming ($I_{\text{obs}} = g^4 I_{\text{emit}}$), causing the approaching side of the disk to appear intensely brightened and blueshifted.
